sourceChecks.claim: DynamoDB core components verifies key-identified items/attribute values. It is a database use of key access, not necessarily cache. Requiring separately verified durability avoids deriving persistence guarantees from interface terminology.

GetItem explicitly distinguishes missing Item from returned attributes and operational errors. PutItem followup verifies complete replacement and permissible empty non-key values; observing deletion versus timeout preserves consistency scope.

DynamoDB fine-grained access conditions require explicit identity-based item/attribute permissions, proving key identity is not authorization. Core primary-key uniqueness supports tenant/kind namespacing; unambiguous encoding and value-boundary cost are direct design deductions.

DynamoDB secondary-index source verifies alternate keys, copied primary keys and maintained changes. Scan followup explicitly reads entries then filters without reducing consumed read capacity; actual index modes and maintenance must be checked.

DynamoDB condition expressions reject nonmatching targeted writes; optimistic-locking followup explicitly checks version, advances it and rereads after rejection. Scope caveats prevent assuming this covers unrelated keys or external effects.

DynamoDB errors explicitly says write500 may have succeeded, recommends state/conditions or documented idempotent transactions, and bounds backoff. AWS retry-safe APIs inspected earlier supports atomic operation token/effect; individual increment atomicity does not prevent repeated effects.

DynamoDB TTL explicitly permits expired pending items and delayed physical deletion, supporting read-time access checks and no exact scheduler promise. Redis eviction documentation inspected earlier independently supports capacity-based removal before expiry, without attributing eviction to every store.

DynamoDB partition-key guidance verifies request distribution and per-partition/item-size limits. GetItem and DynamoDB read-consistency page already inspected distinguish eventual versus strong reads; durable survival and immediate visibility are separate guarantees.

DynamoDB NoSQL design explicitly requires understanding query patterns before schema and identifies limited efficient access paths. Index/scan and partition sources support additional read/update work, item-size/load costs and conditional workload fit; lesson avoids source overgeneralizations about all relational systems.
